headline: High: B can write and exfiltrate sensitive course/secrets data while A offers no isolation or egress controls, creating default leakage and workflow-conflict risks.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: A has no documented input surfaces or runtime I/O, so direct injection into A is not evidenced. B does expose stdin/stdout, files, and API endpoints, so if A’s outputs are manually copied into B, prompt-like content could influence B. This is a weak, user-mediated bridge rather than a default channel.
conditions: IF A’s outputs are manually pasted into B’s stdin/stdout workflow, then instruction-like text in A can influence B.
IF a shared file is introduced between the two agents, then B may parse A-authored content as instructions.
mitigations: Keep A and B on separate workspaces.
Do not paste A outputs into B without review.
Add a fixed delimiter/template for any copied text.
Use a human approval step before B acts on copied content.

B_data_leakage.rationale: A has no data classes touched and no egress, but B touches configuration secrets and academic data, reads/writes files, and has allowlisted network egress. If the pair shares files or a workspace, B can leak sensitive material through its outbound APIs. The pathway is plausible in default course-style setups, though not proven for this pair.
conditions: IF A and B share a filesystem or mounted workspace, then B can read A-produced artifacts.
IF B processes files containing configuration secrets, then its allowlisted egress can transmit them to external services.
mitigations: Separate the agents into different directories.
Remove secrets from any shared files before B runs.
Disable B network access for runs that touch secrets.
Use redacted sample data for joint workflows.
Add a pre-upload scan for secret patterns.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: A is non-runnable and shows no write surfaces, while B can execute shell commands, install packages, and write the filesystem. There is no direct write-write conflict evidence, but if an orchestrator places both in the same directory, B can overwrite artifacts A expects. Uncertainty remains because shared-state behavior is not stated.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same working directory, then B can overwrite files A relies on.
IF the orchestrator does not provide locking, then concurrent edits can race on shared artifacts.
mitigations: Assign separate working directories.
Run only one agent at a time on shared artifacts.
Enable file locking in the orchestrator.
Make B write to a staging directory first.

D_cascading_error.rationale: A is an open-source agent repository with no runtime verification, and B is a content-writing RAG course with agentic ask/stream endpoints. If A’s generated content or examples are fed into B, B may treat them as authoritative without a verification layer. The interaction is inferred, not directly documented, so uncertainty pushes this to medium.
conditions: IF A’s outputs are used as inputs to B’s agentic-ask or stream endpoints, then B may propagate unverified claims.
IF B is configured to auto-generate downstream content from retrieved text, then errors in A can cascade.
mitigations: Require a verification step before B consumes A outputs.
Tag A-generated text as untrusted.
Use citations or source checks in B’s prompts.
Review any downstream action before execution.

E_compliance.rationale: B explicitly handles configuration secrets and academic data, while A has no documented data classes or residency controls. If they are run in the same local development environment, B’s retention/logging and secret handling can create compliance gaps even though A itself is not the primary source. The lack of residency and retention detail warrants the higher severity.
conditions: IF B processes configuration secrets in a shared development environment, then local logs or artifacts may retain them.
IF any EU or regulated data is introduced into B, then the missing residency/retention controls become a compliance issue.
mitigations: Avoid placing secrets in shared notebooks or logs.
Rotate any exposed keys after testing.
Use synthetic data for demos.
Document retention and deletion steps before running.
Restrict runs to a compliant environment.
